title: Approximating the peculiar velocity distribution of dark matter halos with Tsallis statistics
abstract: Dark matter halos, which host galaxies and galaxy clusters, have peculiar velocities far from thermal equilibrium. Characterizing the nonlinear and non-Gaussian features of this velocity distribution improves our understanding of the gravitational evolution of the cosmic web and supports related cosmological applications. We endeavor to establish a connection between the peculiar velocity distribution of halos and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, with the objective of obtaining a model that is both concise and accurate for practical applications. We extracted halo samples from large N-body simulations and performed maximum-likelihood fits to the peculiar velocity distributions using a two-parameter Tsallis model, derived from non-extensive statistical mechanics. On the theoretical side, we reformulated the halo distribution in the superstatistics framework by means of a generalized Gram-Charlier expansion based on the gamma distribution. For halo peculiar velocities below 1000 km/s, the Tsallis model achieves 5 percent accuracy over z=0-2, with performance improving toward lower redshifts. Our results show that the halo velocity distribution becomes increasingly non-Gaussian and departs further from equilibrium over time. The best-fit parameters depend only weakly on mass, though low-mass halos exhibit slightly stronger non-Gaussianity. The two parameters, especially the velocity dispersion, offer promising probes of cosmological parameters. Theoretically, we find that in general the halo peculiar velocity distribution function is expressible as a superposition of a series of Tsallis distribution functions, while simulation results demonstrate that the zeroth-order approximation, namely a single Tsallis function, already achieves sufficient accuracy.
summary: This paper models the peculiar velocity distribution of dark matter halos using Tsallis statistics, a tool from non-extensive statistical mechanics. By fitting simulations, the authors show that the Tsallis distribution accurately captures the non-Gaussian, non-equilibrium nature of these velocities. This provides a powerful, ready-to-use prior for cosmological analyses like kSZ effect measurements.
main_problem: Characterizing the peculiar velocity distribution of dark matter halos, which are far from thermal equilibrium, to improve understanding of the gravitational evolution of the cosmic web.
main_result: The Tsallis distribution provides an accurate and concise model for the halo peculiar velocity distribution, achieving good fit quality for velocities below 1000 km/s across redshifts $z=0-2$.
method: The authors use maximum-likelihood fitting and theoretical superstatistics frameworks to model the non-equilibrium velocity distribution.
model_or_system: The system is dark matter halos in the $\Lambda$CDM model, whose peculiar velocities are analyzed. The model employs Tsallis statistics, derived from non-extensive statistical mechanics, to describe the non-Gaussian nature of the distribution.
key_observables: The one-point distribution function of halo peculiar velocities, $p(v)$, and its moments ($\langle v^{2n} angle$).
important_parameters: The Tsallis parameters, the invariant index $\kappa_0$ and the characteristic velocity $\sigma_{\kappa_0}$.
main_assumptions: The zeroth-order approximation (a single Tsallis function) is assumed to be sufficient, despite the theoretical possibility of a superposition of Tsallis functions. The standard halo model framework is also utilized.
figures_summary: Figures compare the simulated $p(v)$ against the best-fit Tsallis models across different redshifts and halo masses, showing good agreement for low velocities.
paper_structure: The paper develops from the limitations of the standard halo model to the application of Tsallis statistics, deriving the model from superstatistics, fitting it to N-body simulation data, and finally discussing the physical implications of the derived parameters.
why_interesting: The application of non-extensive statistical mechanics (Tsallis statistics) to astrophysical systems like dark matter halos provides a concrete example of how generalized statistical frameworks can model complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in large-scale structure.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Left panel: Halo velocity distribution functions (solid cyan lines) from realization No. 42 of the Quijote fiducial high- resolution simulation at redshifts z = 0, 1, 2. The dashed red lines represent the best fits derived with Eq. 10 with the corresponding (κ0, σκ0) parameters listed in each subpanel. The dotted blue lines represent the best-fit Gaussian models. Right panel: Relative differences between the simulation and the best-fit Tsallis (cyan lines) and Gaussian (blue dotted lines) models. The horizontal dashed red lines indicate the 5% precision level. The velocity bin width is 5 km s−1.

Fig. 2: Left panel: psim (cyan solid) and pfit (red dashed) for the stacked halo samples at z = 0, 1, 2. The parenthetical numbers represent the best fits (κ0, σκ0). Right panel: Relative differences between psim and pfit. The horizontal dashed red lines indicate 5% precision. The velocity bin width is 5 km s−1.

Fig. 3: Comparison of halo velocity moments from the simula- tions with the best-fit Tsallis predictions. In the top panel, data points at different redshifts slightly offset horizontally for clarity. The horizontal dashed red and dotted blue lines indicate 5% and 10% deviation, respectively. In the bottom panel, the Gaussian model, ⟨v2n⟩G, has the same variance as the simulation. The er- ror bars indicate the standard deviations across 100 realizations.

Fig. 4: Quadratic correlation between the velocity components of halos. The symbols represent measurements from the simulation, and the solid line represents the prediction of the best-fit Tsallis model.
